steps.ask: Where does f′ reach its lowest value, compared with its two roots? Which x-value is that?
steps.title: Use the point of inflection

lines.text: $f$ is a cubic, so $f'$ is a quadratic: a U-shape, with its lowest point halfway between its roots.
This is the inflection point of $f$, where the slope is least, and it is given as $\hl{2}{-4}$: $f'(3) = \hl{2}{-4}$.
The lowest point of the graph of $f'$ is $(3, \hl{2}{-4})$.

steps.ask: What is the gradient of p(x) at a turning point? Use that to find two points on p′(x).
steps.title: Read the gradient of p(x) at key points

lines.text: The value of $p'(x)$ is the gradient of $p(x)$.
At $x = \hl{1}{1}$ and $x = \hl{1}{3}$, $p(x)$ has a turning point, so the gradient is $0$: $p'(\hl{1}{1}) = 0$ and $p'(\hl{1}{3}) = 0$.
$p(x)$ is steepest uphill at its inflection point $x = 2$, where the gradient is at its maximum, so $p'(2) = \hl{2}{1}$.
We are given $p'(0) = \hl{2}{-3}$.

steps.ask: Which other point on p′ must sit at the same height as x = 0, and why?
steps.title: Use the shape of p'(x) to find the last point

lines.text: $p(x)$ is a cubic, so $p'(x)$ is a quadratic: a U-shape upside down, with its peak at $(2, \hl{2}{1})$.
A quadratic is symmetric about its peak, so $x = 4$ matches $x = 0$: $p'(4) = \hl{2}{-3}$.

steps.ask: Which points do you now have, and how would you join them into one smooth curve?
steps.title: Plot the points and join them

lines.text: Plot $(0, \hl{2}{-3})$, $(\hl{1}{1}, 0)$, $(2, \hl{2}{1})$, $(\hl{1}{3}, 0)$ and $(4, \hl{2}{-3})$, then draw a smooth curve through them.
